summary:
The first of three letters (1-2 Timothy and Titus, together called the Pastoral Epistles) addressed to individual leaders rather than whole churches. Timothy had joined Paul as a young man on the second missionary journey and became his closest coworker. Now Paul has stationed him in Ephesus, a large and religiously crowded city, to counter false teachers preoccupied with myths, genealogies, and ascetic rules, and to put the church's common life in order. The letter is both a manual and a public endorsement for a younger leader who will need the backing.

Paul's working assumption is that teaching and living rise or fall together. He interrupts the opening charge to offer his own story as evidence of the message Timothy must guard: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst" (1:15). The qualifications for overseers and deacons in chapter 3 are nearly all character rather than credentials — self-control, hospitality, a well-run household — because the church is "God's household... the pillar and foundation of the truth" (3:15). The passages on women's roles and the support of widows are among the most debated in the New Testament; interpreters divide over how much addresses the Ephesian situation and how much applies everywhere.

The final chapter turns to money and contentment. The famous line is precise: "the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil" (6:10) — the love of it, not the money itself. Against it Paul sets godliness with contentment and a charge that sums up the letter: "Fight the good fight of the faith" (6:12).
